questions.stem: An astronomer sums the brightness of 30 stars. Which model is best for this sum?

options.text: Binomial, because there are 30 stars.
options.misconception: confuses number of items with binary trials

options.text: Poisson, because brightness is a rate.
Normal, because a sum of many measurements is approximately normal.
Uniform, because stars are independent.

questions.explanation: A sum of many measurements is approximately normal by the central limit theorem. The number of stars does not make it binomial.
questions.hint: Sums of many measurements tend toward normal.

questions.subject: STATISTICS
questions.topic: Sample size for a normal approximation
questions.learningObjective: Compute a minimum sample size
questions.stem: What is the smallest n such that both np and n(1-p) are at least 10 when p=0.5?
questions.explanation: Both conditions require n*0.5 >= 10, so n >= 20. A slip uses 10 total instead of 10 per side.
questions.hint: Solve n*p >= 10 for p=0.5.

questions.subject: STATISTICS
questions.learningObjective: Detect skewness as a violation

stimulus.body: A histogram of comet tail lengths is strongly right-skewed with a long upper tail.

questions.stem: Is a normal model appropriate for these tail lengths?

options.text: Yes, because the mean can be computed.
No, because lengths are positive.
Yes, because sample size is large.
options.misconception: invokes large n for skewed data

options.text: No, because strong right skew violates normality.

questions.explanation: Strong right skew violates the symmetry of a normal model. A large sample does not remove skewness.
questions.hint: Check the shape of the histogram.

questions.subject: STATISTICS
questions.topic: Using a distribution to answer a question
questions.learningObjective: Compare two values using z-scores
questions.stem: Night A has 16 meteors when mean is 10 and sd is 2; Night B has 22 when mean is 18 and sd is 4. Which night is more unusual?

options.text: Night A, with z=3 versus Night B's z=1.
Night B, because 22 exceeds 16.
Night A, because its mean is smaller.
They are equally unusual, both above their means.

questions.explanation: Night A's z-score is 3, while Night B's is 1, so Night A is more unusual. Raw counts alone mislead.
questions.hint: Standardize both values.

questions.learningObjective: Compute expected value of a function
questions.stem: A random variable X has E[X]=4. What is E[3X+2]?

questions.hint: Use linearity of expectation.

questions.subject: STATISTICS
questions.learningObjective: Identify changing n as misuse
questions.stem: An astronomer models meteor counts over nights but the number of observable hours changes each night.

options.text: Binomial works if hours are averaged.
Binomial works because outcomes are binary.
Binomial fails because the number of trials is not fixed.
Binomial fails because probability varies.

questions.explanation: A fixed number of trials is required; varying observable hours changes n. Averaging does not restore a fixed trial count.
questions.hint: Check whether n is fixed.

questions.subject: STATISTICS
questions.learningObjective: Explain why normal models misfit bounded data
questions.stem: An astronomer uses a normal model for the fraction of the sky covered by clouds, which ranges from 0 to 1. Why is this misuse?

answer.exemplar: A normal model extends below 0 and above 1, but cloud cover is bounded in [0,1], so probabilities outside the range are impossible yet predicted.

questions.explanation: Normal models are unbounded, while cloud cover is bounded between 0 and 1. Predictions outside the support are impossible but still produced.
questions.hint: Consider the support of the variable.

questions.learningObjective: Compute the mode of a binomial
questions.stem: For a binomial with n=7 and p=0.5, what is the most likely number of successes?
questions.explanation: With n*p=3.5, the two central values 3 and 4 are equally most likely; reporting 3.5 represents their midpoint. A slip reports only 3 or 4.
questions.hint: Check the two central values when np is a half-integer.

questions.subject: STATISTICS
questions.learningObjective: Select between normal and binomial
questions.stem: An astronomer records success/failure for 15 nights with p=0.2. Which model is primary?

options.text: Normal, because n is at least 15.
Uniform, because outcomes are equally likely.
Poisson, because p is small.
options.misconception: confuses small p with Poisson necessity

options.text: Binomial, because trials are fixed, binary, and independent.

questions.explanation: Fixed binary independent trials define a binomial model. Small n or small p does not change the underlying model.
questions.hint: Identify the exact model first.

questions.topic: Sample size for a normal approximation
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate a proposed approximation
questions.stem: A note approximates a binomial with n=100, p=0.01 by a normal and says it is fine because n is large.

options.text: The approximation is poor because np=1 is far below 10.
The approximation is fine because n exceeds 100.
The approximation is fine because n(1-p) is large.
The approximation is poor because p is exactly 0.01.

questions.explanation: np=1 is far below 10, so the normal approximation is poor despite large n. The success-failure condition must be checked.
questions.hint: Compute np.

stimulus.body: A boxplot of nightly meteor counts shows several extreme high outliers above 40.

questions.learningObjective: Compute a probability using the normal model
questions.stem: Nightly meteor counts are normal with mean 15 and sd 5. What is the z-score for 5 meteors?
questions.explanation: The z-score is (5-15)/5 = -2. A slip reverses the subtraction or uses the wrong sd.
questions.hint: Subtract mean, divide by sd.

questions.subject: STATISTICS
questions.learningObjective: Compute standard deviation from variance
questions.stem: A random variable has variance 16. What is its standard deviation?
questions.explanation: Standard deviation is the square root of variance, so sqrt(16)=4. A slip returns the variance unchanged.
questions.hint: Take the square root of variance.

questions.subject: STATISTICS
questions.learningObjective: Spot a misuse in a log note
questions.stem: A log note models the number of meteors in 10 minutes as binomial with n=10 and p=0.5.

options.text: This is valid because n and p are specified.
options.misconception: thinks specifying n and p suffices

options.text: This is misused only if meteors cluster.
This is valid because probability is constant.
This is misused because meteors are counts over time, not fixed trials.

questions.explanation: Meteors in a time interval are counts, not a fixed number of binary trials. Specifying n and p does not create fixed trials.
questions.hint: Ask what a trial is.

questions.learningObjective: Compute the expected value of a binomial
questions.stem: For 20 nights with shower probability 0.15, what is the expected number of shower nights?

questions.hint: Multiply n by p.

questions.subject: STATISTICS
questions.learningObjective: Summarize model choice rules
questions.stem: Summarize how an astronomer should choose between binomial, normal, and Poisson models for a new data set.

answer.exemplar: Use binomial for fixed binary independent trials, Poisson for rare events over many opportunities, and normal for sums or means or symmetric quantitative data with large enough samples.

questions.explanation: Each model has distinct requirements: binomial needs fixed binary trials, Poisson suits rare events, and normal fits sums, means, or symmetric data. Choosing by convenience leads to misuse.
questions.hint: Match the data structure to model requirements.
